In addition, the CFPB makes much of the complaint
data public, which is intended to help consumers make informed decisions
about their banks and financial transactions, and also allows researchers to
conduct analyses. Compared to the prior regulatory regime, the establish-
ment of the CFPB complaint database increased the visibility of consumers’
complaints about their banks. Further, given the CFPB’s charges to moni-
tor and respond to complaint data, individual complaints potentially have
an impact beyond any resolution for the complainant. These features
resonate with the setting in Prendergast [2002], where the agent has
an ex ante incentive to avoid investigation—if an investigation occurs,
outside constituencies (who can affect the bank’s welfare) obtain more
information about the bank, whereas in the absence of an investigation,
they observe nothing about bank activities and update positively because
of the lack of complaints. Overall, the establishment of the CFPB increases
reputational costs for banks, both because of the heightened regulatory
threat and because of the publication of consumer complaints. The new
regime also reduces the cost of complaints for consumers and essentially
establishes a credible “principal” in Prendergast’s [2002] model.

3.2 consumer complaint data
   The consumer complaint database published by the CFPB is a collection
of complaints on a range of consumer financial products and services.
In late 2011, the CFPB’s Office of Consumer Response began accepting
and processing consumer complaints. When filing a complaint, consumers
must affirm that the information is true to the best of their knowledge.
The CFPB does not validate the factual allegations of complaints, but it
does take steps, such as asking consumers to supply a verifiable account
number, to confirm a commercial relationship between the consumer and
the bank. The bureau withholds complaints from publication if banks are
unable to verify the commercial relationship or if CFPB staff believe the
complaint was filed by an unauthorized third party. Further, the bureau
consolidates duplicate complaints from the same consumer and intervenes
to clarify ambiguities and anomalies in mass-complaint submissions.
   The database generally updates daily, and complaints are published after
the company responds to the complaint or after 15 days, whichever comes
first.15 Because of privacy concerns, the CFPB discloses very limited infor-
mation about consumers who file complaints. It does, however, provide the
state where the consumer lives and, in most cases, the zip code of the con-
sumer’s mailing address. The complaint data also include information such

15 If the company does not meet the 15-day deadline to respond to a complaint, the bureau

will mark it as “untimely.” The CFPB expects complaints to be resolved within 60 calendar
days.

as the date of submission, the financial institution named in the complaint,
the type of product and issue the consumer identified in the complaint
(including in some cases narrative about the issue), actions the bank took
in response to the complaint, and whether the bank’s response was timely.
   We collect five years of data on consumer complaints, from December
1, 2011, to November 25, 2016. We focus on “meritorious” complaints—
those that were resolved with monetary or other form of relief (134,339
complaints, or 20% of the total). Although the absence of relief does not
necessarily indicate a lack of merit, complaints that did not receive relief
may be partly attributable to consumers’ lack of financial literacy, rather
than to wrongdoing by banks. Because regional variation in financial
literacy could provide confounding variation in the number of consumer
complaints, we exclude these potentially nonmeritorious filings. We investi-
gate the “meritorious” complaints further by collecting data on regulatory
consequences from the CFPB’s enforcement database.16 The database
describes enforcement actions filed in federal court or administrative adju-
dication proceedings against specific financial institutions that result from
CFPB investigations of systematic illegal or improper practices that harm
consumers. For each of the 332 banks that received at least 10 meritorious
complaints, we manually search the enforcement database for information
about penalties and broad-scaled consumer relief paid by the bank.17 We
then examine the relation between the number of meritorious consumer
complaints and the total payments for penalties and consumer relief made
by each bank. The correlation between the number of complaints that
received relief and total enforcement-related payments made by the banks
is 0.31 (significant at 1%), which suggests that the consumer complaints
we study do have merit. Further, the association between complaints and
bank payments is consistent with consumer complaints to the CFPB having
spillover effects that increase the costs of those complaints to banks.
   Table 1 provides descriptive information about the sample of meritorious
complaints. Panel A lists financial institutions that have received at least
1,000 meritorious complaints. Panel B reports the number of complaints
for various categories of financial products or services. The information on
detailed categories is available for 54% of the complaints. About 25% of
the complaints are related to checking or savings accounts. Another 25%
are related to mortgages, and about 10% are related to other types of loans.
The autocorrelation of the frequencies of different categories across years
is 0.94, suggesting that the relative importance of complaint issues remains
stable over time. The complaint issues also seem fairly concentrated within

3.3 summary statistics for complaints, trust, and other
state-level data
   Panel A of table 2 reports summary statistics for the number of com-
plaints at different levels (e.g., by state, by state-year, or by bank-state).
Over the sample period, states average 2,624 meritorious complaints, with
a standard deviation of 3,529. Because some of our tests require data from
the GSS, a personal-interview survey on American society conducted by the
National Opinion Research Center at the University of Chicago, we also
provide summary complaint statistics for the subset of states with available
GSS data. The GSS states average 3,527 meritorious complaints over the
sample period, and 706 meritorious complaints per year. Finally, because
we examine the effect of the WF scandal on non-WF banks, our descriptive
statistics include data about non-WF complaints by state-year and city-year.
   Figure 1 displays the number of meritorious complaints per capita for
each state and Washington, D.C., using red bars, where darker shades of
red correspond to higher complaints per capita. In making the per capita
adjustment, we deflate the number of complaints by the size of the banked
population (i.e., people with bank accounts) in the state. Washington, D.C.,
has the highest per-capita number of complaints, followed by Delaware and
Maryland, whereas North Dakota and Iowa have the fewest complaints per
capita.
   Panel B of table 2 reports summary statistics for state-level variables,
which come from several data sources. Our first measure for trust in the lo-
cal area, GSS Trust 2010, uses the GSS data referenced above.18 The survey,
which includes demographic, behavioral, and attitudinal questions, asks
whether people can be trusted, to which respondents answer either “can
trust” (assigned a value of 3), “depends” (assigned a value of 2), or “cannot
trust” (assigned a value of 1). We then average across all respondents to ob-
tain a state-level measure of trust for 2010, the last year with available data
before the start of our sample period, for 35 states.19,20 We measure trust
at a local level rather than at the individual level both because of data avail-
ability and because the literature on trust suggests that social environment

Chen [2013]).
   19 Analysis of the panel data from 2010, 2012, and 2014 suggests that trust is quite persistent

(autocorrelation is 0.62), with much higher variation across states (0.15) than within states
(0.09).
   20 Cook and Ludwig [2006] suggest that the GSS data are at least capable of providing

representative samples at the census division level. Although we aggregate the GSS data at

and networks are important determinants of people’s attitudes about trust
(Giannetti and Wang [2016], Gurun, Stoffman, and Yonker [2017]).
   We construct state-level measures that capture local demographic infor-
mation prior to the establishment of the CFPB. We use data from the Cur-
rent Population Survey (CPS) to construct the variable Banked 2011, which
measures the number of people age 15 or older with a bank account. The
data used to construct this measure are only available biennially; therefore,
this variable is measured as of 2011.21 The other state-level demographic
information in panel B comes from the 2010 census. Pop 2010 is the total
population of the state. As the correlation matrix in panel C shows, Pop
2010 and Banked 2011 are highly correlated at the state level, so we include
only Banked 2011 in our regression analysis. PercapitaInc 2010 is the annual
per capita income (in 2010 inflation-adjusted dollars) of the state. Male
2010 is the fraction of males in the state’s population. Bachelor 2010 is the
fraction of people 25 years old or older who obtained at least a bachelor’s
degree. MedAge 2010 is the median age of the state’s total population. Mi-
nority 2010 is the fraction of the state’s population that reported a race that
is not “White Alone.” This is the key variable used by Begley and Purnanan-
dam [2018], who examine discrimination against minority customers in
the financial services industry, although they focus on mortgage-related
products or services only. In addition, we construct time-varying versions of
some of these variables to use in panel regression analysis. Banked measures
the number of people age 15 or older with a bank account in a state-year,
and PercapitaInc is the annual per capita income in a state-year.
